---
title: "Measuring natural-parts judgments"
---

We now face the problem left open by the
[UDS response process](generative-stories.qmd): a yes or no response may reflect the
predicate node, the annotator, or Bernoulli variation. A useful model must separate
those sources.

The model covers one part of the event-structure representation in [Gantt, Glass, and White (2022)](https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.2/): the natural-parts gate. Conditional follow-up questions and confidence have no likelihood terms here. Each item identifier anchors one predicate node in one sentence context, so item effects vary over those contextualized nodes rather than verb lemmas or context-free event types.

We begin from the earlier [joint factorization](writing-a-joint-model.qmd), add the
[annotator-specific intercepts](annotator-effects.qmd), and use the
[recovery analysis](parameter-recovery.qmd) to check whether the released incidence
design can separate the two group scales. We then inspect posterior population and
item summaries, check partial pooling and replicated responses, and compare the
fitted item scale with the released normalized values.

## Loading measurements and posterior draws

```{r}
#| label: load-uds-measurement
#| message: false
#| warning: false

uds <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/uds/uds-natural-parts.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)
uds_cache <- readRDS(
  "data/uds/uds-natural-parts-posterior-cache.rds"
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(uds) == 2955L,
  length(unique(uds$item_id)) == 1000L,
  length(unique(uds$annotator_id)) == 12L,
  sum(uds$natural_parts) == 659L,
  setequal(unique(uds$natural_parts), 0:1),
  all(table(uds$item_id) >= 2L),
  all(table(uds$item_id) <= 3L),
  !anyDuplicated(paste(uds$item_id, uds$annotator_id, sep = "::")),
  nrow(uds_cache$population_draws) == 400L,
  ncol(uds_cache$item_effect_draws) == 1000L,
  ncol(uds_cache$annotator_effect_draws) == 12L,
  identical(uds_cache$item_levels, unique(uds$item_id)),
  identical(uds_cache$annotator_levels, unique(uds$annotator_id))
)

uds$item_index <- match(uds$item_id, uds_cache$item_levels)
uds$annotator_index <- match(
  uds$annotator_id,
  uds_cache$annotator_levels
)

design_summary <- data.frame(
  responses = nrow(uds),
  items = length(unique(uds$item_id)),
  annotators = length(unique(uds$annotator_id)),
  yes = sum(uds$natural_parts == 1L),
  no = sum(uds$natural_parts == 0L),
  items_with_two_responses = sum(table(uds$item_id) == 2L),
  items_with_three_responses = sum(table(uds$item_id) == 3L)
)

knitr::kable(design_summary)

uds[uds$item_id == "ewt-test-963%%ewt-test-963-semantics-pred-6",
    c("graph_id", "node_id", "annotator_id", "natural_parts")]
```

Only the raw binary responses enter the likelihood. The released normalized value is retained for an external comparison after fitting.

The displayed rows anchor *exhibited* in “His artworks were selected and exhibited in British Museum in 2002.” The graph-to-sentence mapping follows the [`decomp` graph-ID convention](https://decomp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/data/syntactic-graphs.html), and the sentence comes from the [UD English EWT 1.2 test file](https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_English-EWT/blob/r1.2/en-ud-test.conllu). The three responses—0, 1, and 0—were elicited for one predicate node under the natural-parts prompt. The annotation target is the predicate in this sentence context; the responses do not supply three context-free labels for the lemma *exhibit*.

## Writing the complete model

For each observed pair $(i,j)\in\mathcal O$,

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\alpha+u_i+a_j.
$$

The response rows are conditionally
[independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) after their shared item and annotator
effects are supplied. The scale parameters below are
[standard deviations](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd)
for the raw latent coordinates before centering.

We use the
[non-centered parameterization](../statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd)
introduced on the recovery page: sample a standard-normal coordinate $z$ first,
then multiply it by the unknown group scale $\sigma$ to construct the deviation.
This represents the same conditional normal distribution as sampling the deviation
directly, but gives the sampler different coordinates. The fitted deviations also
center those standard-normal vectors:

$$
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),
\qquad
z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
$$

$$
a_j=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right),
\qquad
z_j^{\text{annotator}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
$$

The priors are

$$
\alpha\sim\mathcal N(0,2.5^2),
$$

$$
\sigma_{\text{item}}\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(2),
\qquad
\sigma_{\text{annotator}}\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(2).
$$

Since the scale parameters are constrained positive in Stan, the normal statements for them induce half-normal priors. Centering fixes both realized effect sums at zero. Thus $\alpha$ is the log odds for an item and annotator at their respective origins, and

$$
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_i)
$$

is item $i$'s yes probability with the annotator coordinate fixed at zero. Integrating over an annotator population instead averages the inverse-logit transformation across possible annotator deviations; the later prediction section computes that distinct quantity.

The zero-sum transformation introduces mild dependence among the realized effects: if one centered $u_i$ increases while the raw-vector mean is held fixed, other centered effects must offset it. The non-centered raw variables remain convenient sampling coordinates, while the centered effects give $\alpha$ a finite-sample origin. Subtracting a realized vector mean imposes that origin by construction; it supplies no empirical evidence that a broader item or annotator population has mean zero.

More precisely, $\sigma_{\text{item}}$ and $\sigma_{\text{annotator}}$ are raw-deviation scales. The induced centered item variance is $\sigma_{\text{item}}^2(1-1/I)$, and two distinct item effects have covariance $-\sigma_{\text{item}}^2/I$; replace $I$ with $J$ for annotators. This finite-population dependence is the consequence of subtracting each raw vector's realized mean.

For observed responses $\mathbf y$, the
[posterior distribution](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd) comes
from Bayes' rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(&\alpha,\boldsymbol z^{\text{item}},
\boldsymbol z^{\text{annotator}},
\sigma_{\mathrm{item}},\sigma_{\mathrm{annotator}}\mid\mathbf y)
\propto{}&
\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal O}
p(y_{ij}\mid\alpha,u_i,a_j)\\
&\times p(\alpha)
p(\boldsymbol z^{\text{item}})
p(\boldsymbol z^{\text{annotator}})
p(\sigma_{\mathrm{item}})
p(\sigma_{\mathrm{annotator}}).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf a$ inside the response factors are deterministic functions of the two raw vectors and their scale parameters, as defined above. Writing the density over the raw coordinates matters: the centered effect vectors lie on zero-sum subspaces and therefore do not have ordinary full-dimensional normal densities. The omitted proportionality constant is the integral of the numerator over every unknown raw coordinate and parameter. Stan does not calculate that integral directly. It generates correlated draws whose long-run distribution is the posterior; posterior medians, intervals, and predictions below are functions evaluated across those joint draws.

The prior choices encode **regularization**: sparse item- or annotator-specific evidence
is combined with a shared population distribution, pulling weakly informed
deviations toward the population center. This is the Bayesian analogue of the
coefficient shrinkage developed in
[ridge regression](../regression-models/ridge-regression.qmd). The intercept prior
permits a broad range of baseline probabilities without concentrating on the
boundary. The half-normal scale priors favor smaller heterogeneity but leave room
for large item or annotator differences. Standard-normal deviations are
**exchangeable**, meaning that item or annotator labels do not predict their prior
ordering; this is the same symmetry introduced in the
[exchangeable Bernoulli model](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd).
They also assume symmetric, light-tailed group populations. A potential worry is
that “weakly regularizing” means inconsequential. It does not: with only two or three
responses per item, prior scale choices can affect item shrinkage.

Before conditioning on the observed responses, we can inspect their combined
implications through a
[prior predictive check](../statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd).
We draw unknown quantities from the prior, generate a complete response table under
each draw, and inspect the resulting yes rates. No observed response is used in this
calculation.

```{r}
#| label: uds-prior-predictive

set.seed(20261102L)
prior_predictive <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(400L), function(draw) {
    prior_alpha <- stats::rnorm(1L, 0, 2.5) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    prior_sigma_item <- abs(stats::rnorm(1L, 0, 2)) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    prior_sigma_annotator <- abs(stats::rnorm(1L, 0, 2)) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    prior_item <- stats::rnorm(length(uds_cache$item_levels))
    prior_item <- prior_sigma_item * (prior_item - mean(prior_item))
    prior_annotator <- stats::rnorm(length(uds_cache$annotator_levels))
    prior_annotator <- prior_sigma_annotator *
      (prior_annotator - mean(prior_annotator))
    prior_rep <- stats::rbinom(
      nrow(uds), 1,
      stats::plogis(
        prior_alpha + prior_item[uds$item_index] +
          prior_annotator[uds$annotator_index]
      )
    )
    data.frame(draw = draw, yes_rate = mean(prior_rep))
  })
)

data.frame(
  statistic = "Prior predictive yes rate",
  t(stats::quantile(
    prior_predictive$yes_rate,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ))
)
```

This check asks whether the prior admits plausible and implausible response matrices before the data are used. A broad interval is not automatically desirable; if substantive knowledge rules out its extremes, the priors should be revised before fitting.

## Fitting the released responses

The [parameter-recovery page](parameter-recovery.qmd) prints the complete Stan program and the exact simulation loop. After the prespecified recovery criteria were met, the released responses were fitted with four separately seeded chains. The fitting call was equivalent to the visible code below; `run_one_chain()` records one chain per seed before the results are combined.

```{r}
#| label: released-uds-fit-call
#| eval: false

stan_program <- '
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> I;
  int<lower=1> A;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=I> item;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=A> annotator;
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> response;
}

parameters {
  real alpha;
  real<lower=0> sigma_item;
  real<lower=0> sigma_annotator;
  vector[I] z_item_raw;
  vector[A] z_annotator_raw;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[I] z_item = z_item_raw - mean(z_item_raw);
  vector[A] z_annotator = z_annotator_raw - mean(z_annotator_raw);
  vector[I] item_effect = sigma_item * z_item;
  vector[A] annotator_effect = sigma_annotator * z_annotator;
}

model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  sigma_item ~ normal(0, 2);
  sigma_annotator ~ normal(0, 2);
  z_item_raw ~ std_normal();
  z_annotator_raw ~ std_normal();

  response ~ bernoulli_logit(
    alpha + item_effect[item] + annotator_effect[annotator]
  );
}
'

model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model(
  cmdstanr::write_stan_file(stan_program)
)

stan_data <- list(
  N = nrow(uds),
  I = length(uds_cache$item_levels),
  A = length(uds_cache$annotator_levels),
  item = uds$item_index,
  annotator = uds$annotator_index,
  response = uds$natural_parts
)

run_one_chain <- function(chain) {
  model$sample(
    data = stan_data,
    chains = 1,
    parallel_chains = 1,
    chain_ids = chain,
    iter_warmup = 800,
    iter_sampling = 800,
    seed = 880000L + chain,
    adapt_delta = 0.95,
    refresh = 0
  )
}

released_chain_fits <- lapply(seq_len(4L), run_one_chain)
```

Four chains permit between-chain convergence checks. The 800 warmup iterations
adapt the Hamiltonian trajectory and mass matrix; the 800 post-warmup iterations per
chain form the full 3,200-draw run. All reported $\widehat R$ values,
[effective sample sizes](../statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd), and
divergence counts refer to that full run. The predictive
calculations below average over 400 joint posterior states, so their finite-draw
Monte Carlo error concerns those calculations rather than the convergence
diagnostics. Revisit [checking Markov chains](../statistical-inference/checking-markov-chains.qmd)
and the [No-U-Turn sampler](../statistical-inference/no-u-turn-sampler.qmd) for the
diagnostic definitions.

## Population summaries

```{r}
#| label: summarize-uds-population

parameter_summary <- uds_cache$parameter_summary[
  c("variable", "median", "q2.5", "q97.5", "rhat", "ess_bulk")
]
names(parameter_summary) <- c(
  "parameter", "median", "lower", "upper", "rhat", "bulk_ess"
)

stopifnot(
  max(parameter_summary$rhat) <= 1.01,
  all(parameter_summary$lower[
    parameter_summary$parameter %in%
      c("sigma_item", "sigma_annotator")
  ] > 0.1)
)

knitr::kable(parameter_summary, digits = 3)
```

Both scale intervals lie away from zero in this model and extract. Predicate nodes vary in their response propensities, and annotators vary in response location after item variation is represented. Because the likelihood contains continuous item deviations for contextualized predicate nodes and no category variable, these intervals support heterogeneity in the annotation process without partitioning predicates into event-structural categories.

The intercept should not be read as the logit of the raw yes proportion. The raw average mixes different item and annotator effects through a nonlinear link, while $\alpha$ locates an item and annotator whose deviations are both zero.

## Seeing partial pooling

```{r}
#| label: plot-uds-partial-pooling
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Raw item proportions and posterior median probabilities with the annotator effect fixed at zero."

item_summary <- uds_cache$item_summary

first_item_zero_annotator <- stats::plogis(
  uds_cache$population_draws[, "alpha"] +
    uds_cache$item_effect_draws[, 1]
)
first_item_average_annotator <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(uds_cache$population_draws)),
  function(draw) {
    mean(stats::plogis(
      uds_cache$population_draws[draw, "alpha"] +
        uds_cache$item_effect_draws[draw, 1] +
        uds_cache$annotator_effect_draws[draw, ]
    ))
  },
  numeric(1)
)

first_item_probability_comparison <- data.frame(
  item_id = uds_cache$item_levels[1],
  estimand = c(
    "Annotator effect fixed at zero",
    "Averaged across the 12 fitted annotator effects"
  ),
  posterior_median = c(
    stats::median(first_item_zero_annotator),
    stats::median(first_item_average_annotator)
  )
)

knitr::kable(first_item_probability_comparison, digits = 3)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  item_summary,
  ggplot2::aes(
    observed_proportion,
    average_annotator_probability_median
  )
) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "steelblue4", alpha = 0.25, size = 1) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 1 / 3, 1 / 2, 2 / 3, 1), # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
    labels = c("0", "1/3", "1/2", "2/3", "1") # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Raw item yes proportion",
    y = "Posterior median item probability"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Most raw item proportions occur at a few fractions because each item has two or three responses. Posterior probabilities occupy a continuous range and move raw endpoints toward the fitted population. This shrinkage reflects both sparse item measurement and the annotator composition of each item.

The displayed first-item comparison keeps two estimands apart. Fixing $a_j=0$ evaluates a coordinate-defined reference annotator. Averaging `plogis(alpha + u_i + a_j)` over the 12 fitted annotator effects integrates over this finite observed annotator set. Because the inverse logit is nonlinear, that average need not equal `plogis(alpha + u_i)`. Neither quantity is a context-free lexical probability.

## Checking replicated response matrices

A fitted ordering is not enough. A
[posterior predictive check](../statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks.qmd)
draws replicated data under parameter values from the posterior and compares chosen
summaries with the same summaries of the observed responses. We generate one
replicated response for every observed item--annotator pair in each posterior draw.
Two summaries target distinct features: the overall yes rate and the proportion of
items containing both response values.

```{r}
#| label: compute-uds-ppc

set.seed(20261103L)
posterior_predictive <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(uds_cache$population_draws)), function(draw) {
    eta <-
      uds_cache$population_draws[draw, "alpha"] +
      uds_cache$item_effect_draws[draw, uds$item_index] +
      uds_cache$annotator_effect_draws[draw, uds$annotator_index]
    replicated <- stats::rbinom(
      nrow(uds),
      size = 1,
      prob = stats::plogis(eta)
    )
    item_sums <- rowsum(replicated, uds$item_index, reorder = FALSE)
    item_counts <- rowsum(
      rep(1L, nrow(uds)),
      uds$item_index,
      reorder = FALSE
    )
    annotator_sums <- rowsum(
      replicated,
      uds$annotator_index,
      reorder = FALSE
    )
    annotator_counts <- rowsum(
      rep(1L, nrow(uds)),
      uds$annotator_index,
      reorder = FALSE
    )
    data.frame(
      draw = draw,
      yes_rate = mean(replicated),
      mixed_item_rate = mean(item_sums > 0 & item_sums < item_counts),
      unanimous_yes_item_rate = mean(item_sums == item_counts),
      annotator_rate_sd = stats::sd(annotator_sums / annotator_counts)
    )
  })
)

observed_item_sums <- rowsum(
  uds$natural_parts,
  uds$item_index,
  reorder = FALSE
)
observed_item_counts <- rowsum(
  rep(1L, nrow(uds)),
  uds$item_index,
  reorder = FALSE
)
observed_statistics <- c(
  yes_rate = mean(uds$natural_parts),
  mixed_item_rate = mean(
    observed_item_sums > 0 & observed_item_sums < observed_item_counts
  ),
  unanimous_yes_item_rate = mean(
    observed_item_sums == observed_item_counts
  ),
  annotator_rate_sd = stats::sd(
    as.numeric(rowsum(
      uds$natural_parts,
      uds$annotator_index,
      reorder = FALSE
    )) /
      as.numeric(rowsum(
        rep(1L, nrow(uds)),
        uds$annotator_index,
        reorder = FALSE
      ))
  )
)

ppc_summary <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    statistic = "Overall yes rate",
    observed = observed_statistics[["yes_rate"]],
    t(stats::quantile(
      posterior_predictive$yes_rate,
      c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    ))
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "Items with both responses",
    observed = observed_statistics[["mixed_item_rate"]],
    t(stats::quantile(
      posterior_predictive$mixed_item_rate,
      c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    ))
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "Items with unanimous yes responses",
    observed = observed_statistics[["unanimous_yes_item_rate"]],
    t(stats::quantile(
      posterior_predictive$unanimous_yes_item_rate,
      c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    ))
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "SD of annotator yes rates",
    observed = observed_statistics[["annotator_rate_sd"]],
    t(stats::quantile(
      posterior_predictive$annotator_rate_sd,
      c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    ))
  )
)
names(ppc_summary)[3:5] <- c("lower", "median", "upper")

stopifnot(
  all(ppc_summary$observed >= ppc_summary$lower),
  all(ppc_summary$observed <= ppc_summary$upper)
)

knitr::kable(ppc_summary, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-uds-ppc
#| fig-width: 7.0
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive distributions. Vertical lines mark the observed statistics."

ppc_plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    statistic = "Overall yes rate",
    value = posterior_predictive$yes_rate
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "Items with both responses",
    value = posterior_predictive$mixed_item_rate
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "Items with unanimous yes responses",
    value = posterior_predictive$unanimous_yes_item_rate
  ),
  data.frame(
    statistic = "SD of annotator yes rates",
    value = posterior_predictive$annotator_rate_sd
  )
)
ppc_observed <- data.frame(
  statistic = c(
    "Overall yes rate",
    "Items with both responses",
    "Items with unanimous yes responses",
    "SD of annotator yes rates"
  ),
  observed = unname(observed_statistics)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(ppc_plot_data, ggplot2::aes(value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(
    bins = 25,
    fill = "grey75",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(
    data = ppc_observed,
    ggplot2::aes(xintercept = observed),
    color = "#2B6F8A",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Posterior predictive statistic", y = "Draws") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

All four observed summaries are compared with their predictive intervals. Mixed and unanimous-yes item rates probe two parts of within-item response composition, while the standard deviation of annotator rates probes between-annotator spread. A model may reproduce the overall rate while missing any of these structures.

## Comparing with the released normalized values

The release also supplies one normalized natural-parts value per item. Those values were not likelihood inputs. The following association compares the fitted and released measurement procedures after fitting.

```{r}
#| label: compare-uds-release

released_comparison <- stats::cor(
  item_summary$average_annotator_probability_median,
  item_summary$released_normalized_value,
  method = "spearman"
)

data.frame(
  comparison = "Posterior item probability versus released normalized value",
  spearman_correlation = released_comparison
)
```

The Spearman correlation is `r format(round(released_comparison, 3), nsmall = 3)`. This association suggests that the compact binary model captures much of the released ordering. It is not a likelihood contribution or a test in which one measurement procedure must defeat the other.

## Limits of the measurement claim

The recovery and predictive gates support one narrow analysis. Six limits remain.

1. The extract deterministically selects 1,000 multiply annotated development and test items. No sampling mechanism gives every UDS predicate, English predicate, or predicate use a known chance of inclusion, so the fitted distribution describes these contextualized items.
2. Most items have three responses, so item probabilities remain strongly regularized.
3. The annotator term represents location only, not discrimination, consistency, or interpretation.
4. The raw confidence serialization conflicts with the documented scale, so confidence is excluded.
5. The available fields do not include raw responses for part similarity, duration, or dynamicity that can be checked against documented response scales; those conditional branches are not fitted.
6. An item is a PredPatt predicate node in sentence context, not a context-free verb lemma.

A potential worry is that passing two posterior predictive checks makes the model adequate for every purpose. While the checks target the rate and within-item disagreement that motivated this model, they cannot validate unmodeled branches or a lexical interpretation of item effects. New targets require new response data and new recovery checks.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the binary response model"}
1. Why is the released normalized value absent from the likelihood?
2. What does the connected item--annotator design make possible?
3. Why can a unanimous item have a posterior probability below one?
4. Which response features do the two predictive checks target?
5. Which measurements remain blocked?

**Answers.** (1) It is an output of another measurement procedure and would double-use information if inserted as a response here. (2) Shared paths through a connected incidence graph help separate item and annotator locations. (3) Two or three unanimous responses do not determine a probability, and partial pooling retains uncertainty. (4) The checks target the overall rate, mixed and unanimous-yes item composition, and dispersion across annotator rates. (5) Raw confidence cannot be reconciled with the documented scale, and the conditional similarity, duration, and dynamicity responses are unavailable.
:::

## Recap

1. The posterior is the product of the observed-pair likelihood and explicit priors, normalized over all unknown quantities and approximated by joint MCMC draws.
2. Prior prediction checks regularization before the data, while posterior prediction checks consequences after fitting.
3. Zero-sum, non-centered effects identify a coordinate system and support computation; they do not turn latent effects into observed properties.
4. A zero-annotator probability differs from an average over annotators because the inverse logit is nonlinear.
5. The next page extends the response process with the [gate-and-branch protocol](gated-annotations.qmd#the-observed-protocol), while keeping unavailable branch data outside the empirical likelihood.
